source: Guillaume, Cramer, van der Torre, Schiltz (2022) Reasoning on conflicting information: an empirical study of Formal Argumentation
finding: 130 young adults drew attack arrows between natural-language arguments and judged acceptability. Attack judgments matched the intended graph; CF2 applied to the intended graph predicted acceptability best and grounded was worst.
numbers: Attack drawing correct: simple reinstatement 82.96% (89.25% after group talk); floating 77.36% to 82.50% (t(11)=2.86,d=0.82,p=.007); 3-cycle 77.40% to 88.12%; the hardest set 63.92% to 80.15%; overall about 80.76% correct. Acceptability prediction (chance 33%): BaseAF-CF2 59.6% first response, 73.6% group, 72.4% final; grounded lowest on all three. On the 3-cycle A and B: of 50 final answers 28 fit CF2, 6 fit preferred, 16 neither.
quote: the grounded semantics systematically yielded by far the worst predictors of all three semantics
limits: Students aged 18 to 36 in Luxembourg, groups of 3 to 5 deliberating, only 3 small AFs (4-5 arguments), 130 people, answers within a group not independent. One attack (recency of citation) was judged bidirectional, not unilateral as intended.
agent_relevance: Humans can state attack edges between short natural-language claims at about 80%. When two candidates tie (floating case) grounded leaves everything undecided and humans do not; S7 should not use grounded alone as the only survivor rule.

source: Cramer and Guillaume (2018) Empirical Cognitive Study on Abstract Argumentation Semantics (full text)
finding: Two pilot studies measured how well people judge attacks between arguments; main study compared grounded, preferred and CF2 on floating reinstatement and a 3-cycle. Grounded failed on floating reinstatement.
numbers: Pilot: designed items judged as intended 74% (students) and 84% (14 expert researchers). Rahwan et al. items judged as intended only 56% and 73%; their intended one-way attacks seen as one-way by only 17% of students and 44% of experts. Main: floating reinstatement, preferred/CF2 predicted 100% and 97.5% of answers (science, maths) vs grounded 0% and 2.5%; news context 67.5% vs 27.5% (p<.001). 3-cycle: CF2 56%, grounded/preferred 12%, none 32%.
limits: Same Luxembourg student group as the 2022 study (earlier version); group deliberation before individual answer; 45, 60 and 25 participants per AF type; world knowledge shifted the news context.
agent_relevance: Edge-judging accuracy depends strongly on how the claims are worded: 17% to 84% across item sets. Our edge judge needs checks on one-way vs two-way attacks, the same weak spot (direction) seen here.

source: Polberg and Hunter (2018) Empirical evaluation of abstract argumentation: supporting the need for bipolar and probabilistic approaches (IJAR; arXiv 1707.09324)
finding: Non-student online participants judged two dialogues step by step. People used many degrees of belief, not accept/reject/undecided, and rarely fully accepted or fully rejected. Classical admissible and complete semantics were the hardest postulates to satisfy.
numbers: Amazon Mechanical Turk, 69 unique participants, 156 entries, about 51% passed language, attention and comprehension screens, 80 valid responses (40 per dialogue). Most used 4 to 6 distinct belief values over a dialogue; chance of 3 or fewer is 0.0000015.
quote: the two (or three) valued perception of acceptance exhibited by the classical Dung's semantics oversimplifies human modelling
limits: No single grounded-match percentage; tests belief postulates, not Dung extension match. Scale of 6 degrees, not 3-state. Only 2 dialogues. About half of entries were screened out.
agent_relevance: Second source, different population (adults online): graded belief beats 3-state labels. Supports keeping a score next to the survive/fall flag in S7. Does not replicate the 75% grounded match.

source: Rahwan, Madakkatel, Bonnefon, Awan, Abdallah (2010) Behavioral experiments for assessing the abstract argumentation semantics of reinstatement (Cognitive Science)
finding: Abstract only (via OpenAlex). Two studies on simple and floating reinstatement. Reinstatement is cognitively plausible but recovery of the attacked argument is not full; floating reinstatement acts like simple reinstatement, which argues for preferred over grounded.
numbers: Not extracted (abstract only). Cramer and Guillaume 2018 report that its intended one-way attacks were seen as one-way by only 17% of students.
limits: Full text not read. Ratings on a 7-point scale, not 3-state.
agent_relevance: Earliest human evidence already disfavoured grounded on floating cases; it agrees in direction with d01 and d02.

source: Experimental evaluation of gradual argument acceptability semantics: the case of reinstatement (Argument and Computation, 2024)
finding: Abstract only. Three experiment variants replicate that reinstated arguments are rated lower than when presented alone; ratings are similar if all arguments shown at once or in sequence; ratings are higher if participants get the theory but still imperfect.
limits: Full text not read. Concludes support at best for 'unattacked is better than attacked', and warns experimenters may read examples differently from humans.
agent_relevance: A real replication of the Rahwan reinstatement effect. Even a defended claim keeps a penalty, so survival after reinstatement should not be scored as fully restored.

source: Cramer and van der Torre (2023) An argumentation semantics for rational human evaluation of arguments (SCF2), Frontiers in AI; re-analysis of the 61-person study
finding: Re-analysis of the earlier study: of 61 participants 12 were incoherent; of 49 coherent, 22 follow a grounded-like strategy and 27 do not. In 11 of 12 AFs most of the 27 non-grounded people agree with CF2; the exception is a six-cycle.
numbers: Six-cycle AF: only 33% of coherent non-grounded participants fit CF2; 60% fit SCF2, stage2, preferred and semi-stable. Stage2 did worse than CF2 on every other AF where they differed.
limits: Reuses one data set (same 61 students). A new semantics (SCF2) fitted to that data, so fit is partly post hoc. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Humans split into two strategies (skeptical vs decisive). Choose the semantics per use: grounded for must-be-safe survivors, CF2 or preferred when ties must be broken. Evidence on larger cycles is thin.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Can formal argumentative reasoning enhance LLMs performances? (MQArgEng)
finding: Pipeline: Mistral-7B writes three answers each with three supporting arguments, itself flags conflicts (attack edges), ASPARTIX computes grounded (or preferred if grounded is empty), and the survivors are fed into a final prompt. Average MT-Bench score rose slightly.
numbers: MT-Bench, GPT-4 as judge: average +2.18% over baseline; better on reasoning, coding, extraction, STEM, humanities (5 of 8 categories), tie on math, worse on writing (8.15 to 8.05) and roleplay-type categories. Table layout scrambled in extraction; exact per-row values not reliable.
limits: Quantised Mistral-7B, one run, human moderator, GPT-4 repeated as judge, no token matching (several extra calls), no cycle statistics reported, baseline added zero-shot CoT. Exploratory.
agent_relevance: Only study that feeds the LLM-judged attack graph to a Dung solver with a fallback rule (grounded, else preferred). Gain small, not token-matched, and the fallback implies empty grounded sets occur.

source: Jin et al. (2026) ARGORA: orchestrated argumentation for causally grounded LLM reasoning, Table 1
finding: Three GPT-4o-mini experts debate into a QBAF tree scored with DF-QuAD. Compared with a compute-matched majority vote of 3 (MV3), accuracy rises on some benchmarks and is about equal on others.
numbers: MMLU-Pro (N=500): direct 0.604, direct MV3 0.604, CoT-like MV3 0.618, ARGORA DF-QuAD 0.638 (post-override 0.636 to 0.642). MedQA (N=500): MV3 and ARGORA both 0.812 (NRE significant p=.032 only). McNemar tests: significant NRE on MMLU-Pro (p=.026 best semantics), MedQA (.032), GPQA (.039 best); TruthfulQA .073, MuSR murder .095 not significant. Best-semantics numbers use ground truth and are an oracle.
limits: Table columns scrambled by pdftotext; only rows checked by name are quoted. Graphs are trees, quantitative semantics, not Dung. Preprint, gains are 2 to 3 points.
agent_relevance: Nearest thing to a token-matched test (MV3 vs 3 experts): small gains, mixed significance, none at ceiling. Partial answer to gap 1: tiny positive at best, not shown for Dung grounded.

source: Jin et al. (2026) ARGORA, ablation H.2 base score initialisation (Table 13)
finding: LLM-assigned task-aware base scores beat a constant 0.5 on accuracy and on net reversal efficiency; with constant scores the override step turned harmful (negative NRE) on GPQA and MuSR tasks.
numbers: MMLU-Pro 0.638 vs 0.618 (neutral); GPQA Diamond 0.523 vs 0.419; neutral NRE negative on GPQA (-0.009), MuSR murder (-0.036), MuSR team (-0.014). TruthfulQA neutral showed p=.005 for NRE, which the authors explain as a binary-task saturation artefact.
limits: No calibration measure (Brier or ECE) of the base scores. Scores come from an orchestrator LLM that also sees the question. Cells read from a scrambled table; MMLU-Pro and GPQA pairs are the sure ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: LLM base scores help here compared with uniform, but are not shown calibrated. Baba and Chudziak (d12) note that base scores and edge polarities in such systems are never checked.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: which yields better decisions in multi-agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Across 7 benchmarks, plain majority voting among agents matches or beats multi-agent debate; debate rounds alone do not raise expected correctness (martingale argument).
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct average accuracy: single agent 0.7205; decentralized MAD T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; centralized MAD T=2 0.6551; majority voting 0.7691. GSM8K: MV 0.9400 vs MAD T=2 0.8867. Arithmetics MV 0.9900 vs best MAD 0.8400.
limits: Debate in natural language, not attack graphs. Same number of agents, but voting uses fewer tokens, so it is cheaper not just equal.
agent_relevance: Token-matched baseline that any S7 survival rule must beat: voting over samples. Gap 1 stays open for attack-graph code, but the bar is voting, and debate alone fails it.

source: Shi et al. (2024/2025) Judging the Judges: a systematic study of position bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: 15 LLM judges, over 150,000 evaluation instances: order of the candidates changes the verdict a lot, more when answers are close in quality; list-wise worse than pairwise for weak judges.
numbers: MTBench pairwise position consistency (PC): GPT-4 0.82, GPT-4o 0.76, Llama-3.3-70B 0.80, Llama-3.1-8B 0.69; repetition stability above 0.95 for best judges (Llama-3.1-8B 0.75). List-wise PC: GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.34, GPT-4o 0.68. PC rises as the quality gap grows; judge identity and task category are significant predictors; prompt length only weakly.
limits: Measures judging of answer quality, not attack-edge labels between claims. Row-to-model mapping of the scrambled table checked for GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: closest measured data. Order flips a judge in 18 to 43% of pairwise cases; close candidates (the ones that matter for S7) flip most. Judge each edge in both orders and keep only consistent edges, or treat flips as mutual attack.

source: Baba and Chudziak (2026) On the LLM verification for argument graph generation
finding: Checks of LLM-built argument graphs should be code first. An LLM reviewer finds injected defects (including cycles) at near ceiling, but objects to correct graphs and changes verdict on identical input.
numbers: 112 human-annotated graphs of 3 to 10 nodes, 404 mutants, 1,548 calls. Recall: field removed 0.96, duplicate id 1.00, dangling ref 1.00, support cycle 0.97. Objects to 11 of 112 correct graphs (9.8%); verdict differs across 3 identical calls on 6.2%; median latency 2,758 ms vs 1 ms for a validator.
quote: gradual semantics computes verdicts from LLM-built frameworks whose base scores and edge polarities are never checked
limits: Small graphs, one reviewer model, preprint (Oct 2026), tests structure not edge truth. Cycles tested are in the support relation.
agent_relevance: Supports code-computed checks at S7 (cycle detection costs 1 ms, LLM check is flaky). Also states the gap we found: nobody validates LLM edge labels or base scores.

source: ArgMed-Agents (2024) Explainable clinical decision reasoning with LLM discussion via argumentation schemes
finding: Generator and verifier LLM agents build an attack graph of decisions; a symbolic solver checks acceptability. Large gains over CoT on two medical sets, and an empty acceptable set is a signal of LLM knowledge limits.
numbers: 300 items per set. GPT-4 MedQA: direct 67.8, CoT 71.4, ArgMed 83.3; PubMedQA 72.9, 77.2, 81.6. GPT-3.5 MedQA: direct 52.7, CoT 48.0, ArgMed 62.1. In 63% of cases with no acceptable decision, identifiable reasoning errors existed; 76% of those from conflicting knowledge.
limits: Multi-round generator-verifier loop (dialogue limit 8), so far more tokens than CoT; no matched voting baseline. Largest gain of any study read here, but not replicated by others.
agent_relevance: Shows a large gain is possible when attacks are specific (verifier tries to attack each decision). Cost unmeasured. An empty result is useful as an abstain flag.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) Creative generation via multi-agent debate: does debate suppress diversity?
finding: Debate pulls agents toward one view and lowers diversity across independent runs. Keeping agents distinct (Creative-MAD) restores it without large quality loss.
numbers: Creative-MAD beats homogeneous MAD by 26.2% (semantic) and 24.0% (lexical) diversity on Qwen3-8B, and 23.3% / 24.0% on Gemma-3-12B; quality within 1.2% and 0.4% of the best method on Qwen3-8B and Gemma-3-12B.
limits: Not formal argumentation and no survival rule. Relevant only by analogy: convergence pressure. 15 runs per setting; small open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: no attack-graph study on open-ended tasks exists. The nearest evidence says convergence-style selection shrinks diversity, so S7 on novelty tasks should only prune candidates that fail an objective test and keep the rest.

source: Ajjour, Quensel, Lipka, Wachsmuth (2026) ArgBench: benchmarking LLMs on computational argumentation tasks (Findings ACL)
finding: 33 datasets, 46 tasks, 11 LLMs. Argument mining (including attack/support relation identification) is hard in zero-shot; few-shot best for large models; quality assessment hardest.
numbers: Macro average across five skills ranges about 0.41 to 0.63 (best 0.633 few-shot); mining scores range about 0.31 to 0.60. Relation identification uses attack or support labels on Peldszus, Stab and Gurevych, Menini and others. Table layout scrambled so per-model rows are uncertain.
limits: Debate-corpus relations (argument units), not relations between candidate solutions. Per-relation F1 not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly closed: attack-edge labelling by open LLMs is far from reliable on benchmark corpora (mining about 0.3 to 0.6), so edge verification matters.

source: Amgoud (2019) A replication study of semantics in argumentation (IJCAI-19 survey)
finding: Survey (not an experiment). Extension semantics give sets, weighting semantics give scores, ranking semantics give orders. Stable can return no extension. Odd cycles make arguments unacceptable under preferred. Scores say how strong, not what to accept.
numbers: No experiments. Examples: stable semantics on an odd cycle has no extension, so no evaluation is possible.
limits: Despite the title, not an empirical replication. Cites Rahwan 2010 and Rosenfeld and Kraus as showing humans do not follow reinstatement fully.
agent_relevance: Confirms that the choice of semantics changes what survives on cyclic graphs and that score semantics need a separate accept rule.

source: Own Monte Carlo (this run): random attack graphs among n candidates, brute-force Dung semantics (script D04.06_sim.py)
finding: If each ordered pair of candidates gets an attack edge at random, cycles are common once edge density passes about 0.2, grounded sets are often empty, and the skeptical preferred set differs from grounded in a fifth of dense cases.
numbers: 5000 random graphs each. n=4: edge prob 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 gives cycle 5.8% / 24.5% / 48.3% / 86.2%; grounded empty 0.6% / 5.6% / 18.7% / 57.8%; multiple preferred extensions 3.8% / 11.9% / 21.9% / 40.3%; skeptical preferred != grounded 0.1% / 2.0% / 7.8% / 22.8%. n=6: cycle 16.8% / 55.6% / 85.2% / 99.6%; grounded empty 0.5% / 9.1% / 32.5% / 81.9%; skeptical preferred != grounded 0.6% / 8.5% / 22.5% / 41.0%.
limits: Random graphs, NOT measured LLM output. LLM edges are not independent or uniform; real density unknown. Not a literature source. It shows sensitivity, not frequency in practice.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no study reports cycle rate of LLM candidate graphs. If a judge labels candidates with mutual conflicts, mutual attack (2-cycles) is the normal case, so grounded alone will often leave all candidates undecided. Log the empty-grounded rate in our own runs.

source: Adaptive Collaboration of Arena-Based Argumentative LLMs for Explainable and Contestable Legal Reasoning (ACAL, 2026)
finding: Multi-agent arena builds argument frameworks for legal tasks and beats debate and RAG baselines on LegalBench-type sets, with uncertainty-aware evaluation helping.
numbers: Learned Hands Courts best accuracy 70.8%, F1 70.7%; Hearsay F1 74.4% (precision 77.1%, recall 76.3%) vs best baseline MAD; an uncertainty component alone gave +7.9 points (64.9 to 72.8); that component alone in another setting 62.8%.
limits: Partial read (results section only). Preprint, graphs and semantics details not checked. Model mix and token cost not equated.
agent_relevance: Another argumentative-LLM result with small gains vs debate, no token match. Counts as same family of work, not independent proof.
